clinicalPearls: Classic triad of hydrometrocolpos (in females), postaxial polydactyly and congenital heart disease
Hydrometrocolpos results from vaginal obstruction with fluid accumulation, presenting as a lower abdominal or pelvic mass in the newborn girl
Affected boys may have genital anomalies such as hypospadias
Caused by biallelic variants in MKKS, the same gene responsible for Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 6
Distinguishing it from Bardet-Biedl in infancy is difficult, because the retinal dystrophy, obesity, learning difficulties and renal disease of Bardet-Biedl emerge only later
Long-term follow-up is essential to detect emerging Bardet-Biedl features and revise the diagnosis if needed
MKKS encodes a chaperonin-like protein contributing to assembly of the BBSome and normal ciliary function
reference.pathophysiology: McKusick-Kaufman syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in MKKS, which encodes a chaperonin-like protein that helps assemble the BBSome, a complex trafficking membrane proteins into and along the primary cilium. Impaired ciliary function during development disturbs the patterning and morphogenesis of the genital tract, limbs and heart, producing hydrometrocolpos, postaxial polydactyly and congenital heart disease. Because the same gene, when more severely affected, causes Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 6, the two disorders lie on a continuum: the additional Bardet-Biedl features of retinal dystrophy, obesity, renal disease and learning difficulties depend on wider ciliary dysfunction and typically appear only with time, which is why the diagnosis may need revision during follow-up.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated hydrometrocolpos (imperforate hymen or vaginal atresia)
additionalInvestigations: Pelvic and abdominal ultrasound for hydrometrocolpos and renal anomalies
Radiographs of the hands and feet for polydactyly
Long-term ophthalmological monitoring, including electroretinography, for emerging retinal dystrophy
Molecular testing of MKKS with a Bardet-Biedl / ciliopathy gene panel
redFlags: A tense abdominal or pelvic mass from hydrometrocolpos causing urinary obstruction or respiratory compromise
Later emergence of retinal dystrophy or renal impairment indicating Bardet-Biedl syndrome
reference.prognosis: With timely decompression of hydrometrocolpos and management of any cardiac lesion the early outlook is good, but if the phenotype evolves into Bardet-Biedl syndrome the long-term prognosis follows that of the retinal and renal disease.
pitfalls: Prematurely excluding Bardet-Biedl syndrome, which shares the MKKS gene and emerges later
Mistaking hydrometrocolpos for other pelvic masses and delaying decompression
Overlooking associated renal or cardiac anomalies
Failing to arrange long-term retinal and renal surveillance
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Prompt drainage and surgical relief of hydrometrocolpos in the newborn girl to correct vaginal outflow obstruction
Cardiological assessment with surgical repair of congenital heart lesions as indicated
Surgical excision of postaxial polydactyly and repair of genital anomalies such as hypospadias in boys
Long-term ophthalmological surveillance with electroretinography for emerging retinal dystrophy
Renal monitoring and attention to obesity and metabolic features should the phenotype evolve towards Bardet-Biedl syndrome
Long-term multidisciplinary follow-up to detect evolving Bardet-Biedl features and revise the diagnosis
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition, with testing of at-risk relatives
